== Problem ==
What is the minimum number of successive swaps of adjacent letters in the string <imath>ABCDEF</imath> that are needed to change the string to <imath>FEDCBA?</imath> (For example, <imath>3</imath> swaps are required to change <imath>ABC</imath> to <imath>CBA;</imath> one such sequence of swaps is
<imath>ABC\to BAC\to BCA\to CBA.</imath>)

<imath>\textbf{(A)}~6\qquad\textbf{(B)}~10\qquad\textbf{(C)}~12\qquad\textbf{(D)}~15\qquad\textbf{(E)}~24</imath>

== Solution 1 (Analysis) ==
Procedurally, it takes:

* <imath>5</imath> swaps for <imath>A</imath> to move to the sixth spot, giving <imath>BCDEFA.</imath>

* <imath>4</imath> swaps for <imath>B</imath> to move to the fifth spot, giving <imath>CDEFBA.</imath>

* <imath>3</imath> swaps for <imath>C</imath> to move to the fourth spot, giving <imath>DEFCBA.</imath>

* <imath>2</imath> swaps for <imath>D</imath> to move to the third spot, giving <imath>EFDCBA.</imath>

* <imath>1</imath> swap for <imath>E</imath> to move to the second spot (so <imath>F</imath> becomes the first spot), giving <imath>FEDCBA.</imath>

Together, the answer is <imath>5+4+3+2+1=\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~15}.</imath>

~MRENTHUSIASM

== Solution 2 (Recursive Approach)==

We can proceed by a recursive tactic on the number of letters in the string.

Looking at the string <imath>A</imath>, there are <imath>0</imath> moves needed to change it to the string <imath>A</imath>

Then, there is <imath>1</imath> move to change <imath>AB</imath> to <imath>BA</imath>.

Similarly, there is <imath>3</imath> moves needed for three letters (said in the problem).

There are <imath>6</imath> moves needed to change <imath>ABCD</imath> to <imath>DCBA</imath>.

We see a pattern of <imath>0,1,3,6,...</imath>. We notice that the difference between consecutive terms is increasing by <imath>1</imath>, so in the same way, for <imath>5</imath> letters, we would need <imath>10</imath> moves, and for <imath>6</imath>, we would need <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~15}</imath> moves.

Thinking why, when we start making these moves, we see that for a string of length <imath>n</imath>, it takes <imath>n-1</imath> moves to move the last letter to the front. After, we get a string that will be changed identically to a string of length <imath>n-1</imath>. This works in our pattern above and is another way to think about the problem!

~world123

Note: 

The sequence consists of triangular numbers shifted a term up (as it starts with <imath>0</imath> on term <imath>1</imath> and <imath>1</imath> on term <imath>2</imath>.)
Thus, our explicit formula is <cmath>\dfrac{(n-1)(n+1-1)}{2} = \dfrac{(n)(n-1)}{2}</cmath> and as <imath>n = 6</imath> in this case (<imath>6</imath> letters), our answer is <imath>\dfrac{(6)(6-1)}{2} = \boxed{\textbf{(D)}~15}</imath> 

~NSAoPS

== Solution 3 (Solution 2 Done Fast)==

We can see that the most efficient way to change <imath>ABCDEF</imath> to <imath>FEDCBA</imath> is the same as changing <imath>ABCDE</imath> to <imath>EDCBA</imath> and then moving <imath>F</imath> to the front in <imath>5</imath> moves. Similarly, this would carry on downwards, where to change <imath>ABCDE</imath> to <imath>EDCBA</imath> would be to change <imath>ABCD</imath> to <imath>DCBA</imath> and move <imath>E</imath> <imath>4</imath> times to the front. This pattern will carry on until <imath>AB</imath> to <imath>BA</imath> would be <imath>1</imath>, and <imath>A</imath> to <imath>A</imath> would be <imath>0</imath>. The answer would be <imath>0(A)+1(B)+2(C)+3(D)+4(E)+5(F)</imath>, which is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~15}</imath> moves.

~Moonwatcher22

== Solution 4 (If you don't notice anything)==
Simply, just blindly doing it, the most straightforward way is to shift F all the way back. From ABCDEF:

<imath>ABCDFE ->ABCFDE ->ABFCDE ->AFBCDE ->FABCDE</imath>

For E:

<imath>FABCED -> FABECD -> FAEBCD -> FEABCD</imath>

For D:

<imath>FEABDC -> FEADBC -> FEDABC</imath>

For C:

<imath>FEDACB -> FEDCAB</imath>

For B:

FEDCBA

That's it, you don't need to do it with A. Still <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~15}</imath> moves.

~pepper2831

==Solution 5 (Inversions of Permutations)==

Let the letters <imath>A, B, C, D, E, F</imath> correspond to the numbers <imath>1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6</imath> respectively. We want to find the number of swaps required to transform the permutation <imath>1 2 3 4 5 6</imath> into the permutation <imath>6 5 4 3 2 1</imath>. 

Here, we let <imath>1 2 3 4 5 6</imath> be the natural order. Then the total number of inversions of the permutation <imath>6 5 4 3 2 1</imath> is <imath>1+2+3+4+5=15</imath>. Hence the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~15}</imath>

~tsun26
